planting.note: Sold as a grafted standard; plant after soil has warmed and stake the graft union through its first year or two.

directions: Umbrella catalpa is a naturally occurring witch's-broom mutation of southern catalpa that is grafted onto a standard trunk, producing a tight, rounded, non-flowering ball of large heart-shaped leaves rather than the tall, flowering form of the species. Because grafted specimens rarely bloom, check the graft union periodically and prune out any upright shoots that revert to the vigorous straight species below the graft. It is widely used as a formal lollipop accent in small courtyards and foundation plantings where a dense, tidy dome is wanted without ongoing shearing. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil and water regularly the first two seasons while the graft and root system establish.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant in spring; locate out of harsh midday sun in hot climates to prevent leaf scorch on the yellow foliage.

directions: Golden catalpa produces the same huge heart-shaped leaves and white, orchid-like summer flower clusters as the species, but new foliage emerges a rich chartreuse-yellow that holds color well into summer before mellowing toward green. Color is strongest with morning sun and some afternoon shade in hot regions, since intense all-day sun can scorch the yellow leaves. Give it room to reach full size, since it grows into as large a tree as the green-leaved species and is not a dwarf form. Prune out any green-leaved reversion shoots from the base promptly, as they grow faster than the golden growth and can overtake it.

planting.note: Plant in spring; most dramatic foliage color shows on new spring growth and on resprouted wood after hard pruning.

directions: Purple catalpa is an old French hybrid between southern and Chinese catalpa, prized for new leaves and shoots that emerge deep blackish-purple before gradually greening through the season, followed by fragrant white summer flowers spotted purple and yellow in the throat. Some growers coppice or hard-prune it in late winter to force a fresh flush of extra-large, intensely colored juvenile foliage at the expense of that year's bloom, similar to the practice used on purple smokebush. Give it full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, since foliage color and vigor both fade in heavy shade. It tolerates urban conditions and brief drought once established but grows best with consistent moisture through its first few seasons.

planting.note: Plant balled-and-burlapped or container stock in spring; tolerates urban soils and street-tree conditions well.

directions: Stately Manor is a male, seedless selection of Kentucky coffeetree bred for a narrow, upright-columnar habit far tighter than the broad-spreading species, making it suited to confined boulevard strips and smaller urban lots. Because it is a male clone, it avoids the large, messy seed pods that the species is notorious for dropping, while still producing the coarse, doubly-compound leaves and winter architectural silhouette the genus is known for. It is slow to establish but, once rooted, tolerates drought, compacted soil, road salt, and alkaline pH better than most shade trees. Plant in full sun with room for its mature height and prune only to remove competing leaders while the central trunk is young.
sources: J. Frank Schmidt & Son Co. nursery catalog

planting.note: Plant grafted or budded stock in spring; this male clone sets no fruit, avoiding the large, sticky hedge-apples of seed-grown trees.

directions: White Shield is a thornless, fruitless male selection of Osage orange chosen for the dense, glossy foliage and tough constitution of the species without the sharp spines or the heavy, inedible green hedge-apples that make the wild tree a litter problem near walkways and mowed areas. It is exceptionally tolerant of poor soil, heat, wind, and drought once established, making it a durable choice for windbreaks, screens, and difficult urban sites where little else thrives. Give it full sun and well-drained soil; it has few pest or disease problems and needs minimal routine care beyond occasional shaping when young. Avoid wet, poorly drained sites, which it tolerates far less well than dry, infertile ground.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in a site sheltered from strong wind and late spring frost, which can damage the large bracts.

directions: This botanical variety of dove tree differs from the typical species mainly in its smooth, hairless leaf undersides and is generally considered hardier and more vigorous in cultivation, which is why most dove trees sold in Western nurseries actually belong to this variety rather than the hairy-leaved type form. In late spring it produces small flower clusters flanked by two large, pure white, handkerchief-like bracts that hang conspicuously along the branches, giving rise to the common names dove tree and handkerchief tree. Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil with shelter from strong wind and afternoon sun in hot climates, since leaf margins can scorch in exposed or dry sites. It can take eight to ten years or more to begin flowering, so treat it as a long-term specimen planting rather than an instant landscape feature.
